issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile and the indexed trauma of witnessed other trauma. Feeling dirty/contaminated is more typical after interpersonal or bodily violation; with the current threat and strategy items, it lacks a plausible clinical link and stands out as an incoherent appraisal for this same trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' implies a broad expectation of impending catastrophe from routine delays, but the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger from strangers and safety behaviors tied to places/people. That mismatch makes this item poorly integrated with the patient's threat theme and coping pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other-trauma profile, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile unless the person had a clear causal role in the event. That degree of personal responsibility is not supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a generalized interpersonal/persecutory danger from unknown people and being followed. In a witnessed-trauma case, this is difficult to reconcile with the appraisals provided, which focus on inadequacy, injustice, and self-blame rather than fear of current attack by strangers.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: 'Watching others closely for signs they might harm me' suggests ongoing expectation of assault. That current threat theme is not meaningfully reflected in the negative appraisals, making the Threat and Appraisal nodes poorly matched despite a strong Threat → Negative Appraisals edge.

issues.item: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
issues.explanation: The threat profile is strongly centered on being followed or intentionally harmed by other people (watching others closely, checking behind, hypervigilance). In that context, 'Avoid Physical Stress' is poorly matched: it implies avoidance of bodily arousal or exertion rather than interpersonal danger, and there are no memory or trigger items supporting a body-stress formulation. Given the available nodes, this strategy appears aimed at a different symptom cluster than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
issues.explanation: 'People Pleasing' can occur clinically, but here it sits awkwardly with the threat items. The threat node describes strangers or others as possible attackers/followers, while people-pleasing implies appeasing immediate social partners to stay safe. Without accompanying appraisals about conflict, angering others, or dependence on keeping people calm, this strategy is not well anchored to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Amira was seventy-one when her daughter called from the hospital. It was a Thursday morning in late spring, and Amira had just finished dressing the Hendersons' two youngest children for school-a routine she had performed five mornings a week for nearly twelve years. The call came as she was wiping jam from a toddler's chin. Her daughter Layla had been walking home from her shift at the clinic where she worked as a nurse, cutting through the park near her apartment as she always did. A man had emerged from behind the trees. What happened next-the struggle, the knife, the way Layla's screams had brought a jogger running-would fracture Amira's sense of safety in a way that no amount of time seemed able to mend.

In those first weeks after the attack, Amira had moved through the Hendersons' house like a ghost. She fed their children, braided their hair, sang to them at naptime, but something essential had withdrawn. The police had arrested a man three days after the assault, but he had been released on bail pending trial. Amira had come to believe with absolute certainty that he was still out there, that the system had failed her daughter, that the people responsible for this failure-the judge, the bail bondsman, the lawyers-would face nothing at all for what they had allowed to happen. This conviction had taken root and would not budge, no matter how many times Layla or her husband tried to reassure her. She was certain that danger was everywhere, that it could emerge at any moment from any direction, and that her vigilance was the only thing standing between her loved ones and catastrophe. The thought of Layla being attacked again consumed her; she imagined it happening to herself, to her grandchildren, to strangers on the street. These images came unbidden and felt impossibly real, as though they were happening in the present moment rather than in her mind.

The park where Layla had been attacked was less than two miles from the Hendersons' home. Amira had stopped driving that direction entirely. What had once been her quickest route to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the mosque where she had prayed for forty years, became impossible. She would take the long way around, adding twenty minutes to simple errands, and even then her hands would grip the steering wheel so tightly that her knuckles turned white. The park itself-she could not go there. She had not walked through it since Layla was a girl. Now the very thought of driving past its entrance made her chest tighten, her breathing shallow and rapid, her heart pounding so hard she thought it might break through her ribs. When she did force herself to drive the main road, she found herself gripping the door handle, bracing as if for impact. At night, she lay awake replaying the details of the assault-details Layla had shared only once, in the hospital-and her mind would construct scenarios of what might have happened if the jogger had not appeared, if Layla had fought back differently, if Amira herself had insisted her daughter take a different route home that evening. She had come to believe, in the darkest hours, that she bore some responsibility for not having prevented what she could not possibly have prevented.

In the months that followed, Amira's world had contracted in other ways. When she was at the Hendersons' house, she found herself watching the children's father with an intensity that surprised her. She noticed the way he stood, the tone of his voice when he spoke to his wife, the angle of his shoulders as he moved through rooms. She was not afraid of him exactly, but she could not stop monitoring him, could not stop searching his face and his gestures for signs of something dangerous lurking beneath. At the grocery store, she watched other shoppers-men especially, but not only men. She watched how they looked at people, where their hands were, whether they moved too close to anyone. Walking from her car to the store entrance, she found herself glancing behind her repeatedly, her neck tense, her breath shallow. Someone might be following her. It seemed important to check. She had also begun to suppress any thought of Layla's attack the moment it surfaced. When an image would start to form-Layla's face, the park, the man's silhouette-Amira would push it away forcefully, redirecting her mind to the children's schedules, to recipes, to anything else. But the effort of this constant mental pushing had left her exhausted. She agreed to things she did not want to do, said yes to plans she dreaded, simply because saying no required energy she did not have. Her husband had invited his brother to stay for two weeks; Amira had wanted to refuse, but the thought of the conflict, the explanation, the risk of disappointing him, had made her simply nod and smile.

It was her youngest grandson, now ten years old, who had finally prompted her to seek help. He had asked why Grandmother never came to the park anymore, why she looked so worried all the time, why she kept checking the windows. In his simple question, Amira had seen herself clearly: a woman living in fear, unable to protect the people she loved most, unable to stop watching for danger that might never come. She had made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that someone could help her understand why Layla's trauma had become her own, and why she could not seem to stop believing that she had failed her daughter, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that her constant vigilance was the only thing keeping her family alive.
